name: The Democrats
subject: It’s not just a bumper sticker slogan
body:
---
Derek, **Here at the DNC, we have a saying: organize everywhere, win anywhere.** To us, that’s not just a bumper sticker saying. It’s something we live every day. That’s why we’re always doing whatever we can to reach the voters who need to hear from us most, through ads, town halls, volunteer contact, social media, and more. We’re always trying new things to expand our reach — like our new program, When We Count, where we are hiring hundreds of young organizers who will spend the next nine months registering thousands of new Democratic voters. We’re investing in state parties and using our networks to assist them with volunteer recruitment. **And here’s the thing: it's _working._** Texas Democrats just flipped a state senate seat in a ruby-red district, in a 32-point swing to the left. That’s not just voters responding to a historically unpopular president; that’s the result of real hard work on the ground. [**So, Derek, can you chip in $7 today to help us continue and expand this work as we gear up for November? #

**Cook Political Report has FOUR U.S. Senate races currently rated as TOSS UPS:** _Georgia. Maine. Michigan. North Carolina._
---

**Georgia’s U.S. Senate seat is currently held by Democrat Jon Ossoff** — _the most vulnerable Democrat in the 2026 midterm elections._ The GOP will undoubtedly do everything they can to win this seat back for a Republican. They’ll spend millions upon millions of dollars. They’ll come up with all sorts of outlandish attacks. Anything to solidify their majority in the Senate next year. **[DEFEND GEORGIA: CHIP IN](https://act.lucaskunce.com/go/100456?refcode=em20260208-10041&firstname=Peter&lastname=Willis&email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=18326&city=Cresco&state=PA&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=1&akid=10041%2E614464%2EZaQaKP)**

Now, we need to make sure we carry the momentum we've seen for Democrats in Maine + across the country all the way to November. **[FLIP MAINE: CHIP IN](https://act.lucaskunce.com/go/100456?refcode=em20260208-10041&firstname=Peter&lastname=Willis&email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=18326&city=Cresco&state=PA&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=2&akid=10041%2E614464%2EZaQaKP)**

**Michigan’s U.S. Senate seat is currently held by Democrat Gary Peters,** who announced that he will retire after his current term. _The good news is that Democrats currently hold every statewide seat in Michigan._ But defending this critical Democrat-held Senate seat won't be easy. _In 2024, Michigan’s U.S. Senate race was one of the closest in the country._ So now, we can absolutely expect the GOP to go all-in to win this open seat. **[DEFEND MICHIGAN: CHIP IN](https://act.lucaskunce.com/go/100456?refcode=em20260208-10041&firstname=Peter&lastname=Willis&email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=18326&city=Cresco&state=PA&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=3&akid=10041%2E614464%2EZaQaKP)**

**North Carolina’s GOP-held U.S. Senate seat is one of Democrats’ top pick-up opportunities for 2026.** We have a strong Democratic candidate in former governor Roy Cooper, who has a record of winning + delivering for the people of North Carolina. _But outside groups are already pouring MILLIONS of dollars into this Senate race!_ If this is any indication, the GOP will spend BIG to stop Democrats from flipping this Senate seat. **[FLIP NORTH CAROLINA: CHIP IN](https://act.lucaskunce.com/go/100456?refcode=em20260208-10041&firstname=Peter&lastname=Willis&email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=18326&city=Cresco&state=PA&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=4&akid=10041%2E614464%2EZaQaKP)**

body:
Phil Weiser’s ICE portal: A hotline for the wrong crisis
| | | | [](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)
---
**February 8, 2026** **SUNDAY NEWS DIGEST**
| |
---
Dear Rocky Mountain Voice family,
With primary season approaching, Rocky Mountain Voice is helping bring candidates directly to voters through a Colorado Republican Candidate Forum in Durango on Feb. 13, featuring moderated panels with candidates for state offices, the U.S. Senate, and governor.
**Have a question for Colorado’s Republican candidates?**
As part of our election coverage, we’re inviting voters to submit questions for consideration at the upcoming Colorado Republican Candidate Forum. Questions submitted through the form will be reviewed by moderators and may be asked live during the event.
👉 **Submit your question[HERE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
With that in mind, here’s what we’re watching — and reporting on — this week in Colorado.
We’re starting with a question of priorities — and a policy choice that reveals a great deal about where Colorado’s leadership is directing its attention.
Attorney General Phil Weiser has launched a new public-facing portal inviting Coloradans to report alleged “misconduct” by ICE agents. Framed as an accountability and transparency measure, the portal does not address a gap in enforcement. [As our editorial board explains](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.), it instead redirects attention away from pressing public safety challenges the state actually has the authority to fix.
Colorado communities continue to grapple with repeat offenders cycling through the system, organized retail theft, fentanyl trafficking, probation failures, and violent crime that too often ends in preventable loss. Yet rather than focusing on those failures, the attorney general has chosen to build a complaint system aimed **at federal agents he does not supervise and cannot discipline.**
That distinction deserves scrutiny.
ICE enforcement in Colorado largely involves individuals already convicted of serious crimes — including violent assault, sexual exploitation, drug trafficking, and gang activity. At the same time, violent crime has declined in several key categories statewide.
**That raises an obvious question: if public safety is improving, why devote state resources to monitoring the enforcement arm some credit with helping stabilize conditions?**
The answer may lie less in oversight and more in politics. The portal coincides with ongoing litigation in which Colorado officials are defending the state’s sanctuary framework against federal challenge. In that context, it reads less like neutral oversight and more like an effort to stigmatize and constrain immigration enforcement through public pressure rather than law.
We encourage you to read [the full editorial](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.). Whether you agree with its conclusions or not, it lays out a clear case for why Colorado’s approach to immigration enforcement deserves closer scrutiny — and why initiatives like this reveal priorities more than they solve problems.
As always, our goal is to give you the context to judge for yourself.
— Team RMV
| | |
---
| | **TOP STORIES OF THE WEEK**
---
**[Phil Weiser’s ICE portal: A hotline for the wrong crisis](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY RMV EDITORIAL BOARD, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) _Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser wants you to do something._ _Not vote. Not volunteer. Not show up to a school board meeting and read the agenda before somebody else reads it for you. He wants you to report ICE._
**[Griswold blocks DOJ voter roll review while data flows elsewhere](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY LINDA GOOD, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) _Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold wants the public to believe that a lawful voter-roll records request from the U.S. Department of Justice is an unprecedented threat to voter privacy. That framing is not principled. It’s strategic._
**[Parents allege school mistreatment of autistic child as Cherry Creek faces federal civil rights investigation](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY SHAINA COLE, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) In response to concerns raised by a family in Colorado about the treatment of their young son in kindergarten, the Office for Civil Rights of the U.S. Department of Education opened an investigation into whether the Cherry Creek School District was in compliance with federal civil rights and special education law, a problem that is not new to the district.
|
---
**LEGISLATIVE SESSION**
Republicans at the Capitol wasted no time drawing contrasts with the Democratic majority this week. In the Senate, Republicans opposed [SB-004](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.), the expansion of Colorado’s red flag law, warning Democrats rejected even basic amendments — including one to protect domestic violence survivors from having the law weaponized against them — while also advancing Senator Liston’s [nuclear workforce development bill](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) as a long-term energy solution. In the House, Republicans focused on local control, public safety, and bipartisan measures honoring veterans, strengthening agriculture, and increasing government transparency. For weekly, unfiltered updates from the Capitol, readers can sign up for Colorado House Republicans’ newsletter [](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)[here]() and Colorado Senate Republicans’ updates [here](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.).
**[Colorado Senate moves to widen red flag authority despite due process warnings](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY SHAINA COLE, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) SB26-004 cleared the Colorado Senate on Feb. 3, passing on a 20–13 vote and moving to the House for further consideration. Sen. Nick Hinrichsen the only Democrat to oppose it. The bill revises the state’s Extreme Risk Protection Order system, often referred to as red flag orders, and prompted extended debate during second reading the day before final passage.
**[Colorado Democrats Advance Immigration Accountability Bills After National Protests](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** [DENVER7](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) On the heels of protests that erupted across the nation related to federal immigration enforcement in Minnesota, Colorado Democrats announced legislation they contend will protect civil rights.
**[Colorado Bill Would Let Select Housing Projects Bypass Local Zoning Rules](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** [DENVER7](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) A bill that would allow certain groups that own land — like schools and affordable housing nonprofits — to avoid certain local-level zoning restrictions is heading to committee.
**[READ MORE ON LEGISLATIVE SESSION](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
|
---
**STATE**
**[More People Are Leaving Colorado as High Costs and Regulations Take Toll](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** [COLORADO POLITICS](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) It’s finally happened. Buried in all the self-congratulatory reports about Colorado reaching the 6 million mark in population last year was news that should be keeping our political leaders up at night. For the first time in 20 years, more people left Colorado to go to other states than moved here from elsewhere in the country, 12,100 more.
**[Colorado Confirms 14th Wolf Death Since Voter Mandated Reintroduction](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** [COLORADO POLITICS](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) The 14th wolf to die in Colorado since their reintroduction about two years ago took place during a “collaring” operation in the northwestern region of the state last week. Colorado Parks and Wildlife said the wolf, identified as #2305 — meaning it was one of the original 10 animals that came from Oregon — died on Jan. 28 in Routt County.
**[Colorado ag department seeks dismissal of whistleblower complaint over DEI as employee calls for HR director removal](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY JEN SCHUMANN, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) More than two months after a single chat comment during a virtual meeting sparked a whistleblower complaint at the Colorado Department of Agriculture, the case has escalated into a legal standoff, with the department moving to dismiss the complaint as the employee seeks the removal of its HR director.
_**[READ MORE STATE NEWS](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**_
|
---
**NATIONAL**
**[ICE Operations Hampered in Colorado and Minnesota After Activists Aid Child Rapist and Gang Member](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** [FOX NEWS](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is detailing cases in which anti-ICE agitators actively helped criminal illegal immigrants evade federal arrest, including suspects accused of child rape, domestic abuse and gang-related violence.
**[House GOP Forces Vote on Citizenship Checks and Photo ID for Voters](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** [JUST THE NEWS](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) The U.S. House of Representatives will vote [this] week on a new bill that would require all states to check both citizenship and photo identification before allowing voters to cast ballots, combining two widely popular election integrity provisions and ramping up pressure on a Senate that has been unwilling to consider either mandate.
**[Rep. Anna Paulina Luna Signals GOP Will Go It Alone To Pass Funding Bills](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** [WASHINGTON EXAMINER](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) House Republicans will attempt to pass the remaining spending bills and the two-week extension funding the Department of Homeland Security along party lines to end the partial government shutdown, Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-FL) revealed on Sunday night.
_**[READ MORE NATIONAL NEWS](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**_
|
---
**LOCAL**
**[Colorado School Accused of Teaching Students to Track ICE Agents](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** [TOWNHALL](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) A presentation was allegedly given at a Jefferson County, Colorado public school instructing students on how to document ICE agents conducting operations. The information included the often-used acronym “S.A.L.U.T.E.” to instruct their children on how to ensure full documentation of the activity of federal agents, essentially equipping them to work as “ICE watchers” like Renee Good and Alex Pretti.
**[Greeley-Evans School District Nurse Reprimanded Over ICE Protest Email](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** [COMPLETE COLORADO](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) While businesses closed, teachers called in sick and students walked out of class across Colorado as a sign of solidarity with two recent shootings by Immigration Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Minnesota, one Greeley-Evans School District 6 staffer decided to push her political opinions onto colleagues via the district email system, earning her a sit down with human resources about the appropriate use of school resources.
**[DUI arrest tests public trust as Aurora councilman keeps safety oversight role](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY SHAINA COLE, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) When an elected official is arrested, the expectation is simple: the law should apply the same way it would to anyone else. But public office brings added scrutiny that doesn’t disappear once the legal process begins. Those questions are now front and center in Aurora following the DUI arrest of Rob Andrews, who serves on City Council and chairs the council’s Public Safety, Courts, and Civil Service Committee.
**_[READ MORE LOCAL NEWS](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)_**
|
---
**COMMENTARY**
**[Ballot Measure 95 Gives Colorado Voters A Say on Sanctuary State Policies](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** [THE GAZETTE EDITORIAL BOARD](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) _Shooting deaths in Minneapolis involving Immigration & Customs Enforcement’s operations have stirred strong opinions about what to do with illegal immigration in our state and across the country. Many Coloradans are against ICE’s operations in Minneapolis and elsewhere, including here in Colorado, under President Donald Trump and find them to be unwarranted and dangerous._
**[Lawmakers admit the problem: One-time money built permanent government](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY CORY GAINES, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) _I wanted to share the Sun article below, but perhaps not for the usual reasons._ _If you read it you’ll note what I and many others around the state have been harping on for some time now. The state has been living beyond its means._

**[Medicaid billing error cost Colorado tens of millions, officials acknowledge](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY CORY GAINES,[ ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) _HCPF really did accidentally pay millions in Medicaid claims. In an earlier op ed about Colorado’s Medicaid expansion (see the first link below) and how that puts our state at higher risk of fraud, waste, and/or abuse, I asked the Colorado Division of Healthcare Policy and Financing, HCPF, the state unit which adminsiters Medicaid, about what they do to prevent or stop such problems._
**[READ MORE COMMENTARY](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
|
---
**Feel like you have a unique story or commentary to share?** Email [submit@rockymountainvoice.com](mailto:submit@rockymountainvoice.com).
|
---

**Boysko Bulletin: Week Four Report From Richmond**
---
Dear Peter, This week was a powerful reminder of what is possible when people come together. I was honored to see so many individuals travel to Richmond for the Walk for Peace and to hear the teachings of the Venerable Buddhist monks. Their message was clear: if we don’t work to create peace within ourselves, we will not have a truly peaceful society. Inner peace extends outward, strengthening families, communities, and relationships even in times of disagreement. As the 2026 session moves forward, that mindset continues to guide my work. Unity makes us stronger, and it is this belief that fuels my commitment to advancing legislation that reflects the values and needs of our community. On Friday, February 6th, Governor Spanberger signed my bill, SB 449, advancing the constitutional amendment to protect the fundamental freedom to make decisions for ourselves regarding the full scope of reproductive healthcare. Now voters across the Commonwealth will have the ultimate say through a ballot referendum in November. It has been an honor to carry legislation that affirms the ability of women and their families to have private, informed conversations with their healthcare providers about reproductive options. I’ve been working on issues surrounding reproductive health for my entire adult life - from marching on Washington as early as 1989 to serving on the Board of Directors for Repro Rising’s predecessor NARAL Pro-Choice VA, to carrying reproductive freedom legislation year after year in the General Assembly. These deeply personal decisions belong in the exam room and not in the hands of politicians. The Constitutional Amendment, SR1, and the accompanying ballot initiative language, SB 449, bring us closer to honoring that principle. Another bill I gave deep and thoughtful consideration to was SB 339. This legislation would allow a mentally capable adult diagnosed with six months or less to live to request that an attending health care provider prescribe self-administered aid-in-dying medication. I did not approach this bill lightly. Many of my constituents asked me to carry this legislation. They want a measure of control and dignity at the end of life, rather than being forced to endure the full progression of a terminal disease as their quality of life diminishes, often forced to endure excruciating pain when medication is no longer effective. Drawing from my own personal experience, I understand the profound impact these illnesses have on individuals and families. The intent of SB 339 is to place decision-making back in the hands of the patient—ensuring that compassion, autonomy, and personal freedom guide end-of-life care, rather than the disease itself. This past week, SB 339 did not advance out of the full Senate committee. I want to sincerely thank every stakeholder, advocate, and individual who took the time to speak on this bill. Their dedication and willingness to share deeply personal perspectives made this important conversation possible. While the legislation did not move forward, I believe we are making meaningful progress by engaging in these difficult but necessary discussions. I am grateful to my colleagues on both sides of the aisle and to all of the people who came to testify for their thoughtful participation and for approaching this issue with care, respect, and compassion. I will continue the work to support and represent our district to the best of my ability, and I look forward to the work ahead throughout this year’s session. I’ve enjoyed your visits, appreciate your calls and emails, and look forward to continuing to stay in touch. Kindest regards,

I am honored to work with the Virginia branch of **Compassion & Choices** this session to advocate for peaceful end of life healthcare options. The Compassion & Choices volunteers have worked year round educating legislators by sharing their personal experiences. Although the bill failed to report from the Committee, we will continue to advocate for people facing the most difficult end of life struggles. Compassion & Choices is a national organization dedicated to informing, empowering, advocating for, and defending patients at the end of life. Its mission is centered on improving care through meaningful systemic and policy change. This work includes developing patient-directed end-of-life care demonstration projects, providing continuing medical and professional education, and advancing federal legislative and regulatory reforms. These efforts focus on improving care for individuals living with dementia, addressing inequities in end-of-life healthcare, and transforming the emergency room experience for patients nearing the end of life. By 2028, Compassion & Choices aims to ensure that at least 50 percent of Americans live in states where medical aid in dying is authorized and accessible. The organization is working to authorize medical aid in dying in additional states, establish pathways toward access in larger jurisdictions, integrate this option into standard patient-directed end-of-life care, and repeal the Assisted Suicide Funding Restriction Act. Ultimately, Compassion & Choices seeks to ensure that every individual is informed, empowered, and engaged—so they can direct, access, and receive end-of-life healthcare that reflects their values, priorities, and dignity. clean_body: | | | Boysko Bulletin: Week Four Report From Richmond Dear Peter, This week was a powerful reminder of what is possible when people come together. I was honored to see so many individuals travel to Richmond for the Walk for Peace and to hear the teachings of the Venerable Buddhist monks. Their message was clear: if we don’t work to create peace within ourselves, we will not have a truly peaceful society. Inner peace extends outward, strengthening families, communities, and relationships even in times of disagreement. As the 2026 session moves forward, that mindset continues to guide my work. Unity makes us stronger, and it is this belief that fuels my commitment to advancing legislation that reflects the values and needs of our community. On Friday, February 6th, Governor Spanberger signed my bill, SB 449, advancing the constitutional amendment to protect the fundamental freedom to make decisions for ourselves regarding the full scope of reproductive healthcare. Now voters across the Commonwealth will have the ultimate say through a ballot referendum in November. It has been an honor to carry legislation that affirms the ability of women and their families to have private, informed conversations with their healthcare providers about reproductive options. I’ve been working on issues surrounding reproductive health for my entire adult life - from marching on Washington as early as 1989 to serving on the Board of Directors for Repro Rising’s predecessor NARAL Pro-Choice VA, to carrying reproductive freedom legislation year after year in the General Assembly. These deeply personal decisions belong in the exam room and not in the hands of politicians. The Constitutional Amendment, SR1, and the accompanying ballot initiative language, SB 449, bring us closer to honoring that principle. Another bill I gave deep and thoughtful consideration to was SB 339. This legislation would allow a mentally capable adult diagnosed with six months or less to live to request that an attending health care provider prescribe self-administered aid-in-dying medication. I did not approach this bill lightly. Many of my constituents asked me to carry this legislation. They want a measure of control and dignity at the end of life, rather than being forced to endure the full progression of a terminal disease as their quality of life diminishes, often forced to endure excruciating pain when medication is no longer effective. Drawing from my own personal experience, I understand the profound impact these illnesses have on individuals and families. The intent of SB 339 is to place decision-making back in the hands of the patient—ensuring that compassion, autonomy, and personal freedom guide end-of-life care, rather than the disease itself. This past week, SB 339 did not advance out of the full Senate committee. I want to sincerely thank every stakeholder, advocate, and individual who took the time to speak on this bill. Their dedication and willingness to share deeply personal perspectives made this important conversation possible. While the legislation did not move forward, I believe we are making meaningful progress by engaging in these difficult but necessary discussions. I am grateful to my colleagues on both sides of the aisle and to all of the people who came to testify for their thoughtful participation and for approaching this issue with care, respect, and compassion. I will continue the work to support and represent our district to the best of my ability, and I look forward to the work ahead throughout this year’s session. I’ve enjoyed your visits, appreciate your calls and emails, and look forward to continuing to stay in touch. Kindest regards, Jennifer B. ## ICYMI: Congressman Morgan Luttrell Endorses Jon Bonck for TX-38

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE Contact: press@jonbonck.com Date: February 9, 2026
HOUSTON, TX -- With just a little over one week before early voting begins, momentum continues to build behind Jon Bonck's campaign for Congress as Morgan Luttrell formally endorsed Bonck for Congress.
"I'm proud to endorse Jon Bonck for Congress in Texas' 38th District. Jon is a proven conservative who understands service, responsibility, and the importance of strong family values, and what it means to fight for the people you represent. Redistricting moved the lines, and Jon will soon represent many of my former constituents. They deserve strong, principled leadership, and I know Jon will fight for them every day. Take good care of them, Jon, they are great Texans!!"
"I'm honored to have earned Morgan Luttrell's support," Bonck said. "Morgan is a great Texan who has dedicated his life to his family, his country, and serving Texas families. I'm running to defend the Trump agenda, secure our border, protect our Christian values, and fight for the great people of TX-38."
With early voting just days away, Bonck has established himself as the clear Conservative and front runner in the race, earning support from across the conservative movement -- including Senator Ted Cruz, Harris County Commissioner Tom Ramsey, Congressman Jim Jordan, Congressman Brandon Gill, Congressman Tim Burchett, and many others.
That support also includes 47 Republican precinct chairs across the district, underscoring the grassroots strength behind the campaign as it enters the final stretch.
Early voting begins February 17, with Election Day on March 3.
For more information or to get involved, visit [www.jonbonck.com](https://47x7wwhbb.cc.rs6.net/tn.jsp?f=001rkh5h3N-kCq2a5UB_ArwVHCXplgX6BdGtuHmzDziqonKC_xJzaJOoVoPCtRvX_X3nC4ZimnljPqGlQo9T6pjWjv5YUAWcxogxdM5hCQTbEfPEhIVemKnW72AEVf4Bwg3b9HXG01ogQbtUDaVhe36zw==&c=_hp5liTQ90K5QkPqOMWjHVkd2dPzrEV1nBNtLjHAr6zMTCeAGMF4DQ==&ch=XqShNhrd7OSDc3qqNcKNIzn3oKo6emk1_SSG2T8bzlgyQG2cvNV9zQ==)

## Super Bowl LX: Seahawks Smother Patriots
A [dominant defensive performance](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0L2uozAQBeCnMZ3RMPwYChfb0GXbLdEEj4M3BiPbiZe3X-XqvsGtP-nonPPnttzIeXc8ftPOOtuwHFyS55w5Lolpo_JMxR2PGFaO1xndyokWBBwkoIRpMeT8tXSV0ZYZua1YN0rB0PYwDdWmV9ONoJSClce2pYb53rcKDY5kmsGuldOfNECYmga6vq0nAjsh8WDuYAcC0QEbl0Os_wZ35I2tv8KbY72GvfJ6y_lMov0lcBY4l1JqTufxQYHzYb3AOeUQL4HzInB2RuDcqVGhgv5j3yNlys56libSk-VOF8uTcnQhJ7nSmV-RZXqdHOU9FC_9vypqcxbnvUuDEh08dnL-q1P-0ZFvjf8DAAD__-1miI0) carried the Seattle Seahawks to a 29-13 win over the New England Patriots in Super Bowl LX, securing the franchise's second Super Bowl title. Seattle running back Kenneth Walker III was named [Super Bowl MVP](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LFuwyAQgOGnwVui80HADAyVKqYma0fras4xLTER0Lh--yp9ha7_8A3_-3k8U0xxvV7oxq7NeVx5q4lb4zJWpoW2r7rF9VryxGW_lzhxpREB9QHwAHYMFNM-qi64mRlZdux6Y0DLE1jdLc5OxhqpB2VmtP0wDAMQSQqoTA_EoYvuqQGC7XtQJ3m0BLNFYh0-YNYEQgGH2HI5fua4toXntOcHl-OUb11yS2v3KuSLQC_Q_zyrQH_xbwJ9bdS-q0CPgGBAGWXsYBVgD1pIX4V8ReiKC_ctphSrNkLB9UYx_eHtX0ceDn8DAAD__4WGcCQ) after rushing for 135 yards on 27 carries. Quarterback Sam Darnold threw for 202 yards and one touchdown. Seahawks kicker Jason Myers [set a Super Bowl record](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0DFygzAQQNHTiM6eZQGJLVSkoYrdpmTW1sookZFHUky4fca5QtpfvOJ_nOYThxjW25nvYqtP8ypbiVKr5LkIL7x9lS2st5yukvdHDlcpPCOgPgAegGbHIe5z3zjrRVC6RmxrDOhuANLNYh1CPw4XGS_eGYMkuqOREfuWRqHRNcG-NECgtoV-6I7E4AlZtLuA1wyqB3Ghpnz8TGGti_i4p6fk4zXdm2iXWh9FdW8KJ4XTz6sqnM7Tu8KpVK7fReGEgKAJTWdoQAQ9amqydY8txBiKNqqH251D_DPrv0Y8Lf4GAAD__0rcbl4) with five field goals, and he supplied all 12 of Seattle's points through three quarters. New England managed just 78 yards and no points entering the fourth. The scoring opened up in the fourth quarter with 30 combined points, including a [defensive touchdown](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0DFywyAQQNHToM6e1SKBKSjSqIrdpmTWYrFIsPAAsaLbZ5wrpP3FK_7H2Z0pprjeLnRn20J2K281cWtcXGVaaPuqW1xvJc9c9keJM1dyCKgOgAcwzlNMuxs6bwMzsuzY9lqDkiMY1S02hKB00DD6E_UkrwNIHueA3ox-nGXoon1pgGD6HoZRHg1BMEis_BWCIhADsI8tl-NnjmtbOKQ9P7kc53zvkl1ae1Qh3wROAqefVxU4XaZ3gVNt1L6rwAkBQRlptB60NHDS-tQV6x9bTClWpcUAtzvF9Ge2f414WvwNAAD__xBpb0Q) that put Seattle up 29-7 with less than five minutes left. The halftime show featured Bad Bunny, who performed in Spanish, with an appearance by Lady Gaga. Meanwhile, Turning Point USA--the organization founded by the late Christian conservative activist Charlie Kirk--hosted its own _[All-American Halftime Show](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LFq8zAUBeCnkbcYWbJla9DwQ8jwQwothUIXcWNdxWoVK0g3Ee7Tl3Ts2vU7cA6ct6M9QohhPT_BBQ35ZFesJSIRZlsQFqifpYb1nNOMebvmMGMBK7hQOy52XFsHIW62b5zxiAJlg6YbR67kwLVqFjMOk-49KDfJsT_pqdMjCD2JfvTeoR-aYB5tXHDddbwfZKuBey0AlTtxr4CznqMLlHL7kcJKC_q4pTvmdk6XJpqF6FqY_MfEgYlDrbXd0o1uJ3zkDwGaFyYPdyb36__ydXzV9Z2emVAxFGJy__KLC0Emm8GFxOS-a7Jx1xpiDEWNrOfnC4T4s01_OuxuxHcAAAD__1cwf1M)_ on social media, headlined by Kid Rock, Brantley Gilbert, and others.
## Lindsey Vonn's Olympic Dream Ends
Lindsey Vonn's pursuit of an Olympic medal ended with a broken left leg following a crash just 13.4 seconds into Sunday's downhill final at the Milan Cortina Winter Olympics. [Follow live updates here](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkDGupDAQRE8DGagxjBkHDjYhm003RI3dHnrX2Mi2xuL2K770T_CzkqpUpXp_XusL2XN4_8aDdHFxDVSzp1IorZlwx_ovVw7vFA2l60xsKOMqQMgORAdqtcj-WqfWakckaGxJD_MMcnyAku2ucTDOinF-OrQWUEk3bmSsdKi2mWZqWd9tIEANA0yPsVcITgkkaTdwEqGZgCyXmPq_kUPZyfkrfij1Jh6t13spZ27GX41YGrHUWvuwmfvF7TdiyWdMJTdiif46Tja39Bxspqv7xBA6G2vY2fuuciiUuu9cl0xA8ZjV8GyTtmdl7znLuZngfSD7r_3yI2gfLf4HAAD__zv2hJ0). The 41-year-old American, who was skiing with a ruptured ACL sustained just nine days earlier, clipped a gate and tumbled down the slope before being airlifted to a hospital, where she [underwent surgery to stabilize](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLFuhDAQRL_GdCCz-My5cJGG7tKmRAtejk2MfbKts_j7iPxCupFGmtF7X4_5gew5PD_xIFu2OAeq2VMplOZMuGP9yZXDM8WV0vlKvFLGGSToVkIrzeyQ_TmrxtmNCGhoyPbjKPVwk0Y3ux2VvqPpcVS902q5u2EgMG5RMG66l6phe61JkKbvpboNnUG5GUDSbpGbRimUJMclpu47cig7bf6Mb0rdGo_G272UVxbDh4BJwFRr7dYlXxRXL2C6ooDJc3CZzvYdQ2hdrGFn79uDPYbYrjEVDihgapJ1r8rec9ajUPJ5IPu_p_IvPW8LvwEAAP__O756uA) the fracture. Her teammate Breezy Johnson [won gold in the race](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLFytCAURp9GOxxERS0o_sZu_zalc4WL3g2CA2QZ8_SZzSuk_-abc87HY30AOfL7fzhRZRtWjyU5zBnjmhAOKJ-pkN9j0BjvK5LGBKvgQjIuGJ9XA-Tuta-NsogCuxpVO45cdgOfZX0oHKCdhmmckE-bbLVujZWDnrteWymsrkm937jgc9vyfuiaGbidBaA0G7cSeNVzNJRDbJ6BfD7Quju8MDY6nLVTR85Xqrp_lVgqsZRSGr_p4O7zIp3em0osb6lKLHBiJA2ebRHx-2bPcPgUPCvkEzOh-IOcY3twhjnyJuHNXsF7BhQd2YyG6fAVEzKwGSPTEdJRR2WuQs5RkmPV8_0Ecr9o-U89X0r8BAAA__9FJY77), becoming only the second American woman to claim Olympic downhill gold after Vonn's 2010 Vancouver victory. The 30-year-old Wyoming native, who missed the 2022 Olympics with a knee injury, held off Germany's Emma Aicher by just four-hundredths of a second. [Watch her ride here](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLFytCAURp9GOxxERS0o_sZu_zalc4WL3g2CA2QZ8_SZzSuk_-abc87HY30AOfL7fzhRZRtWjyU5zBnjmhAOKJ-pkN9j0BjvK5LGBKvgQjIuGJ9XA-Tuta-NsogCuxpVO45cdgOfZX0oHKCdhmmckE-bbLVujZWDnrteWymsrkm937jgc9vyfuiaGbidBaA0G7cSeNVzNJRDbJ6BfD7Quju8MDY6nLVTR85Xqrp_lVgqsZRSGr_p4O7zIp3em0osb6lKLHBiJA2ebRHx-2bPcPgUPCvkEzOh-IOcY3twhjnyJuHNXsF7BhQd2YyG6fAVEzKwGSPTEdJRR2WuQs5RkmPV8_0Ecr9o-U89X0r8BAAA__9FJY77). Vonn had been attempting to become the oldest Alpine skier ever to win an Olympic medal despite competing in a knee brace on the course she loves most, where she's won 12 World Cup races.
## Map: Super Bowl Stars' Hometowns
More than half of the nearly 100 athletes playing in Super Bowl LX [hail from just seven states](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLuOpDAQAL_GZEaNeZ0DB5eQzaUXosZuoHcNRrZnvPz9avYXNi9VSfX_MT-QPZ_bPzzI5DXMJ5XkKWeKcyLcsXymwucWg6V4X5EtJZwVqEGCkqBnh-zvuaucWYkUtRWZZhxhaHvQQ7WbZez_wEioWw3O6lZr7GFpVxgs2oZcxeZtAwW6aaDr21ojrFohDW6BdUAQHZDjHGL9EfjMO63-Di-KtQ1H5c2e85VE-1eoSaiplFJHQv_GbTiEmtC92JJQ0_K8hZrS86Iol1C89F9y522Xye4heJnR05nlxRd5PkkeeAk1VdG4q7D3nIZRdLAdyP4nnX_162XUdwAAAP__FpOBHg), with Texas claiming the most players who played high school football in the state. Texas leads with 15 players, followed by California with 13 from Los Angeles alone. On this day in 1942, U.S. Congress imposed daylight saving time across the nation. Designed to better conserve fuel and other resources during World War II, the time change was originally called . As many of us were watching the Super Bowl from couches and living rooms across the country, aboard the International Space Station were watching the same game from about 250 miles above Earth after NASA beamed Super Bowl LX to the orbiting crew. Save up to 80% on your favorite brands with today's sponsor, ! | Super Bowl LX: Seahawks Smother Patriots A carried the Seattle Seahawks to a 29-13 win over the New England Patriots in Super Bowl LX, securing the franchise's second Super Bowl title. **Good Morning My Fellow Angry Patriots.**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/53d7c2f7-fc9f-42f5-87f4-4df5f562b22a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
When I ran for [Congress in 2022 and again in 2024](https://substack.com/redirect/0612e855-1a5d-428a-89ad-ab6d0d2de988?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), one of my first priorities was campaign finance reform. Not because it is a fashionable talking point, but because once you experience the system from the inside, it becomes impossible to ignore how distorted and unhealthy it really is.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..e0hRu9o77nw2r4UTPlgXqWpuPGvtgCwvEXLhIWCOuAM?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=187205754)
Campaign finance in the United States is completely unmoored from anything resembling democracy. Super PACs, corporations, lobbyists, and massive pools of money dominate elections to the point where messaging, priorities, and even candidate viability are warped before voters ever get a real choice. It does not just distort outcomes. It distorts who even gets to participate.
What this system actually incentivizes is not good governance or good ideas. It incentivizes shaking hands in the right rooms, making promises to people with money, and building the best donor network possible. The candidates who succeed are not necessarily the most thoughtful or capable. They are the ones who can raise the most money, the fastest, and then spend it to overwhelm voters with persuasion.
Campaigns cost money. Mail costs money. TV ads cost money. Digital ads cost money. Organizing volunteers costs money. And the logic becomes circular. If the way to win is always more money, then the skill you are really selecting for is the ability to raise and spend endlessly. Fiscal restraint never enters the picture. Creativity never enters the picture. Guardrails disappear.
#### Politics is a Mega Industry
We like to talk about public service, but let's be honest about scale. In a presidential election year, the amount of money flowing through American politics can exceed the revenues of the NFL, and the combined revenue MLB, and the NBA. Which is fucking crazy.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/99a6c0c6-f99c-4b9c-bbaa-82623f6edf1a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
2024 cycle estimated combining all campaign, party, PAC, outside/independent expenditures, and projected late-cycle ad spending
When you frame it that way, it becomes clear what we are dealing with. This is not civic engagement. This is an industry. A massive one. Bigger than some of the most powerful entertainment businesses in the world.
Citizens United threw gasoline on that fire. It opened the door to even more spending and even more corrupt relationships between politicians and donors. I do not care if you are a Democrat or a Republican. If you cannot look at this system and see a problem, then you are either willfully blind or deeply invested in keeping it exactly as it is.
#### The Lie of Grassroots Funding
Please Think about Becoming a Paid Subscriber
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..e0hRu9o77nw2r4UTPlgXqWpuPGvtgCwvEXLhIWCOuAM?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=187205754)
There is another part of this that frustrates me deeply. The reliance on individual donors. Average people. People who already pay taxes, already struggle with mortgages, rent, healthcare, childcare, car payments, and the basic cost of living.
These same people are constantly asked to open their wallets again. And when they do, campaigns brag about small-dollar donations as proof of grassroots support. The message is that the average person is powering change.
That story is misleading at best.
Campaigns use donation mixing tactics to lower their average contribution numbers. Big donors give large sums. Smaller donations are layered in to make the math look better. It creates the appearance of broad-based support while the real influence remains concentrated where it always is.
When those candidates take office, whose calls do you think get answered? It is not Kathy from rural Ohio who donated fifty dollars and wants to talk about her small soybean farm, unless it is a good photo op. It is the landowner with thousands of acres. The executive. The donor tied to a Super PAC. The person who can offer more than moral support.
That is not conspiracy. That is how incentives work.
#### Why I Support Publicly Funded Elections: My Math
This is why I support publicly funded campaigns at the federal level. And I am specifically talking about House and Senate races here, not state or local elections.
Here is how I think it should work.
Primaries remain privately funded. Candidates raise money, talk to donors, make their case, and earn their party's nomination under existing campaign finance limits. That process stays competitive.
Once the primary is over, the general election changes. The winners receive public funding to run the remainder of their campaigns. No outside money into the campaign itself. No personal fundraising arms race. Just a defined budget and clear rules.
Importantly, this should not mean dumping millions of dollars into a candidate's bank account. Instead, it should work on a credit system administered through federal oversight. Campaign expenses are submitted, verified, and paid through that system. Receipts are uploaded. FEC VISA card issued to candidate. Public campaign finance lawyers available for free. Spending is transparent. Abuse is harder and punishable.
#### A Publicly Funded Alternative That Actually Works

#### What Senate Races Would Actually Cost
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/34781432-bf21-4205-9c72-4deb7deb796f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Not all races are equal, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest.
Here is how this works using your framework.
Start with a base Senate budget of $15 million.
Small media markets would receive approximately 70% of that base.
That puts a race like Iowa at roughly $10.5 million per candidate.
Mid-sized markets would sit around 100% of the base.
That puts a race like Ohio at roughly $15 million per candidate.
Large media markets would receive up to 167% of the base.
That puts a race like California at roughly $25 million per candidate.
That funding would apply only to the general election, and only to the candidates on the ballot. No additional fundraising allowed.
#### What House Races Would Actually Cost
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/e22fe36c-4f26-42a3-946c-d60af9654370?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
House races scale down similarly.
Start with a base House budget of $1.5 million.
Small rural districts would receive closer to $700,000 per candidate.
Mid-sized districts like Cleveland-area seats would receive around $1.5 million per candidate.
Large urban districts in places like Los Angeles, New York City, or Chicago would receive up to $2.5 million per candidate.
Every candidate runs within those limits. No one buys dominance through donor networks. Everyone competes on ideas, organization, and execution.
Obviously these numbers can be tweaked. But you get the idea.
**The Total Price Tag**
There are 435 House races every two years.
Only about one-third of the 100 Senate seats are up each cycle.
When you run the numbers using this model, the total cost to publicly fund all federal general elections every two years comes out to roughly $4 billion.
That is a lot of money. But it is also not outrageous.
We already tolerate far more money influencing elections indirectly through Super PACs, dark money, and regulatory capture. This system would be cheaper, cleaner, and more honest.
#### What We Get in Return
Publicly funded general elections would force candidates to work within constraints. They would have to prioritize. They would have to organize creatively. They would have to speak to voters instead of donors.
It would reduce donor capture.
It would improve candidate quality.
It would strengthen democratic legitimacy.
Is it perfect? No.
Is it better than what we have? Without question.
If we value democracy, we should be willing to invest in it directly instead of letting it be auctioned off.
If we do not, then we should at least be honest about the system we are defending.
I know this is not easy. Overturning Citizens United would likely require a constitutional amendment or a Supreme Court shift. That is a separate fight.
But if we do nothing, the trajectory is clear. Corporate money, Super PACs, foreign influence, and dark funding will continue to expand. Politics will become even more of an industry. And democracy will continue to hollow out.
Publicly funded campaigns are not perfect. But they are a step toward restoring accountability, improving discourse, and putting candidates on something closer to equal footing.
If we value democracy, we should be willing to invest in it. If we do not, then we should at least be honest about what we are choosing instead.
**What are your thoughts?**

Campaign Finance Reform is Needed | | | Feb 9 | | | | | | | | | | | | Good Morning My Fellow Angry Patriots. | | ---|---|--- When I ran for , one of my first priorities was campaign finance reform. Not because it is a fashionable talking point, but because once you experience the system from the inside, it becomes impossible to ignore how distorted and unhealthy it really is. Campaign finance in the United States is completely unmoored from anything resembling democracy. Super PACs, corporations, lobbyists, and massive pools of money dominate elections to the point where messaging, priorities, and even candidate viability are warped before voters ever get a real choice. It does not just distort outcomes. It distorts who even gets to participate. What this system actually incentivizes is not good governance or good ideas. It incentivizes shaking hands in the right rooms, making promises to people with money, and building the best donor network possible. The candidates who succeed are not necessarily the most thoughtful or capable. They are the ones who can raise the most money, the fastest, and then spend it to overwhelm voters with persuasion. Campaigns cost money. Mail costs money. TV ads cost money. Digital ads cost money. Organizing volunteers costs money. And the logic becomes circular. If the way to win is always more money, then the skill you are really selecting for is the ability to raise and spend endlessly. Fiscal restraint never enters the picture. Creativity never enters the picture. Guardrails disappear. Politics is a Mega Industry We like to talk about public service, but let's be honest about scale. In a presidential election year, the amount of money flowing through American politics can exceed the revenues of the NFL, and the combined revenue MLB, and the NBA. Which is fucking crazy. | | ---|---|--- 2024 cycle estimated combining all campaign, party, PAC, outside/independent expenditures, and projected late-cycle ad spending When you frame it that way, it becomes clear what we are dealing with. This is not civic engagement. This is an industry. A massive one. Bigger than some of the most powerful entertainment businesses in the world. Citizens United threw gasoline on that fire. It opened the door to even more spending and even more corrupt relationships between politicians and donors. I do not care if you are a Democrat or a Republican. If you cannot look at this system and see a problem, then you are either willfully blind or deeply invested in keeping it exactly as it is. The Lie of Grassroots Funding Please Think about Becoming a Paid Subscriber There is another part of this that frustrates me deeply. The reliance on individual donors. Average people. People who already pay taxes, already struggle with mortgages, rent, healthcare, childcare, car payments, and the basic cost of living. These same people are constantly asked to open their wallets again. And when they do, campaigns brag about small-dollar donations as proof of grassroots support. The message is that the average person is powering change. That story is misleading at best. Campaigns use donation mixing tactics to lower their average contribution numbers. Big donors give large sums. Smaller donations are layered in to make the math look better. It creates the appearance of broad-based support while the real influence remains concentrated where it always is. When those candidates take office, whose calls do you think get answered? It is not Kathy from rural Ohio who donated fifty dollars and wants to talk about her small soybean farm, unless it is a good photo op. It is the landowner with thousands of acres. The executive. The donor tied to a Super PAC. The person who can offer more than moral support. That is not conspiracy. That is how incentives work. Why I Support Publicly Funded Elections: My Math This is why I support publicly funded campaigns at the federal level. And I am specifically talking about House and Senate races here, not state or local elections. Here is how I think it should work. Primaries remain privately funded. Candidates raise money, talk to donors, make their case, and earn their party's nomination under existing campaign finance limits. That process stays competitive. Once the primary is over, the general election changes. The winners receive public funding to run the remainder of their campaigns. No outside money into the campaign itself. No personal fundraising arms race. Just a defined budget and clear rules. Importantly, this should not mean dumping millions of dollars into a candidate's bank account. Instead, it should work on a credit system administered through federal oversight. Campaign expenses are submitted, verified, and paid through that system. Receipts are uploaded. FEC VISA card issued to candidate. Public campaign finance lawyers available for free. Spending is transparent. Abuse is harder and punishable. A Publicly Funded Alternative That Actually Works | Senate Public Financing By State V24.04KB ∙ PDF file ---|--- | | House Public Financing By State5.54KB ∙ PDF file ---|--- | What Senate Races Would Actually Cost | | ---|---|--- Not all races are equal, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Here is how this works using your framework. Start with a base Senate budget of $15 million. Small media markets would receive approximately 70% of that base. That puts a race like Iowa at roughly $10.5 million per candidate. Mid-sized markets would sit around 100% of the base. That puts a race like Ohio at roughly $15 million per candidate. Large media markets would receive up to 167% of the base. That puts a race like California at roughly $25 million per candidate. That funding would apply only to the general election, and only to the candidates on the ballot. No additional fundraising allowed. What House Races Would Actually Cost | | ---|---|--- House races scale down similarly. Start with a base House budget of $1.5 million. Small rural districts would receive closer to $700,000 per candidate. Mid-sized districts like Cleveland-area seats would receive around $1.5 million per candidate. Large urban districts in places like Los Angeles, New York City, or Chicago would receive up to $2.5 million per candidate. Every candidate runs within those limits. No one buys dominance through donor networks. Everyone competes on ideas, organization, and execution. Obviously these numbers can be tweaked. But you get the idea. The Total Price Tag There are 435 House races every two years. Only about one-third of the 100 Senate seats are up each cycle. When you run the numbers using this model, the total cost to publicly fund all federal general elections every two years comes out to roughly $4 billion. That is a lot of money. But it is also not outrageous. We already tolerate far more money influencing elections indirectly through Super PACs, dark money, and regulatory capture. This system would be cheaper, cleaner, and more honest. What We Get in Return Publicly funded general elections would force candidates to work within constraints. They would have to prioritize. They would have to organize creatively. They would have to speak to voters instead of donors. It would reduce donor capture. It would improve candidate quality. It would strengthen democratic legitimacy. Is it perfect? No. Is it better than what we have? Without question. If we value democracy, we should be willing to invest in it directly instead of letting it be auctioned off. If we do not, then we should at least be honest about the system we are defending. I know this is not easy. Overturning Citizens United would likely require a constitutional amendment or a Supreme Court shift. That is a separate fight. But if we do nothing, the trajectory is clear. Corporate money, Super PACs, foreign influence, and dark funding will continue to expand. Politics will become even more of an industry. And democracy will continue to hollow out. Publicly funded campaigns are not perfect. But they are a step toward restoring accountability, improving discourse, and putting candidates on something closer to equal footing. If we value democracy, we should be willing to invest in it. If we do not, then we should at least be honest about what we are choosing instead. MAGA has declared war against free and fair elections.
For months, Defend Our Courts has warned that MAGA was plotting to rig upcoming elections by any means possible. What Bannon revealed confirms exactly the type of extreme measures that we feared: they are preparing to use federal force to interfere with voting itself.
MAGA knows it is headed for major losses if elections remain free and fair. Instead of changing course, it is choosing coercion. Instead of persuasion, it is choosing fear.
And it's important to be clear about how this works.
In most states, the presence of law enforcement at polling places is tightly regulated--or prohibited entirely--by state law. The authority to stop voter intimidation does not come from Washington. It comes from state courts, and ultimately from state Supreme Courts.
That is why MAGA's long-term strategy has focused on capturing those courts. This is not new. This is the next phase.
Last year, Defend Our Courts helped lead the successful defense of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court--a critical firewall in the most important swing state in the country. That victory wasn't symbolic. It protected the court that would have final say over election disputes in 2026 and beyond.
Now MAGA is escalating nationwide.
In 2026, state Supreme Court elections will take place in Michigan, Wisconsin, and Georgia--the very states where voter intimidation would be most consequential, and where courts will be called on to intervene if MAGA follows through on its threats.
This is why Defend Our Courts exists. We saw what was coming early. We rallied over 100 thousand Democrats to support our cause and built a winning model in Pennsylvania.
Now we are taking our winning formula national. With Democrats stretched thin by House and Senate races, defending democracy in the courts will not happen unless we do it.

## 3,000 Wind Turbine Parts Litter Sweetwater
A lawsuit filed on behalf of the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality accuses Washington-based Global Fiberglass Solutions of [dumping](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkDFuhDAQRU8DndFgJoALF2noNm1KNF4PYMnYCJtluX3EXiHdFPOe_v-_j_FBzrsw_9DKOr-nOAY-k-eceR-9y4s71s1TyHHjkNLzMORCGiXIVoAUoEZLzl8jllYbsKouWdddB23TY4vloieaTENA0PZfHXWm5r6rsW-U6hXg1JVO3zKQoGoJNcgKe4U9YoNKIRjkAoGty3Gv8sKZ35Qmf8UX79UzrqXXS85bKprvQg6FHM7zrKb4xrvG_VDI4T4LOXxQkQ5O4nTBinzsxgUWz7huFC5B3vPM1l-CDAUbgwuzaABAGE_2pjhl8bGUu7bb6bx3qe0KhHkl5z9x8v9GfGn5FwAA__90hYhh) more than 3,000 wind turbine components at two sites in Sweetwater. The facilities contained 487,000 cubic yards of solid waste as of last March, according to the lawsuit. The company was not permitted to store components, and it has [failed to recycle](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyk0LGOpDAQBNCvMZlHjfEADhxcQraXXojauGexZAxyN8vM359mfmHzqqdS_fuavzDlVL7_4kZeno99LnRxJhGqc06ypnM7MhbZDyrMyxkwFZ4NmF6D0eDmiCm_ZttEHyC6tiHfDgP03Wh726w-3JE6a5fh3kWMMIZ7cDi4vhvhMY5D2yT_xsCAaw20YG52dHa0trPOWQiWlAWKSfZ6k5WEnsiP_Np_qN6WfWuyX0UOVt0fZSZlpog5I9PzqMT8TigzsaCQMtOnrPkk1lcqUctZQyqkKy2vJVPVb1V3AKBDxkis47kdFHUqmi8iuVCoKjM11cfjSjkn7gdl4XvDlD9z5Hcn_njzPwAA__-V1IhL) at least 75% of its accumulated material each year. Attorney General Ken Paxton is seeking an injunction requiring the [removal of waste](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyk0DGupDAQBNDTQGbUNB7AgYNNyP6mGyKDm6ElY5DdDMPtVzNX-Aeop6r69zP-OA4cn3_dRlbeyz5GunIgEUpjYFn53I7gouwHxZznc3Ic84iArQJUYEbvONyjLr2dwJu6JFt3HbRNr1tdrvbRzQ1CPfvHw3Q9da6rqVkW7FFrBNOWbD8YIJgaoQasdG90r3WjjdEwaSo0kGfZUyUrCb1dXsK9vyhV876Vwa4iRy6aPwUOBQ4UKT3vz4iJnFTzXuDwDal8UlYXR6_kTBNHUonmew6U1EdTDQCoKThPWflzO8grjipfRHI5oVTgUCbrj4tD4Nx2hYbn5jh8a8jvzntZ_B8AAP__0U2E9w) within 180 days and civil penalties between $50 and $25,000 per day for each alleged violation, some of which date back to 2017. "_Just because the radical left calls something a 'green industry' does not give any company a free pass to harm the Texas countryside, break our laws, and leave Texans to deal with the negative impacts_ ," [Paxton said](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkDGupDAQRE8DmUfG08uMA4JNyP6mG6LGbqAlYyPc_v7cfsVcYeNXeqqqv1_TF3LguP7BnQb5WdIUqeZAInROgWXjsh8Bo6SDYs6uzMgxT0abXmmjtJ08crgmaP0wa2-7lobu9dL98w09tNug0XUWsScHBG-P0OECTwsA_tcLrGt5uGXaaNsZ3WnzgLeFN8ATrAU9AzWgybOk8yEbCf1gXsKVvul8uLS3YdhEjtw8fzdmbMxYa33MvLpUopzXlnY6cKU72pjx3taYMQsKqbSoj03lQlm5tB8YL4XOlUz-phwCrRjCpXzZD46rki2VjNHnG1eOXkk5Z46k5oCesuKociWSikJnY8b2HPxROQTO_asBve7I4dNb_u_t78H8CwAA__85MJlj) in a statement.
## Lithium Extraction Plant Opens in Midland
Gov. Greg Abbott joined a host of state and federal officials Friday for a ribbon-cutting ceremony at Fort Worth-based Element3's new [lithium extraction plant](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyk0LHOozAQBOCnMR1osRdiFy6uocu1VyITL2ElYxDehOTtT4n-N_jrkWb0zb_reA2cON__hpW8vOZtzHSWRCJ0jIll4ce6p5Bl2ymXcntMgXMZNei-Bl2DG2Pg9B6xin6C6NqKfHu5QG8s9lgtfopxBojW4WzbHk1v7NR1SK5zluYAFftPGWhwrYYWdIPWoUU06BzChKQQKLJsRyMLCb1CmdN7e9LR3La1Sn4R2Ysyf5QelB7O82zWQz6Z0sP0KJypFKWHcAjfEik9UKKVsph6p2PlkOsfZ_2F1ro1xna6bfZlrw4f95NT4tJfFMJ9DZy-u_K7t55e_w8AAP__DnZ-nw) in Midland. The lithium carbonate production facility is the first in the U.S. to extract the valuable resource from oilfield wastewater. The Permian Basin's oil and gas industry produces about a billion gallons of wastewater every day, which is "full of critical materials" and [represents](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkMGupCAURL8GdxhEHuqCxWzcvdnO0iBc2ptcwQi07d9PetKZH3jLSqoqderP9_JtkTA-ftsdTHmFtES4MkEpcC6EZcO6H2RjSQfEnF1dLca8SCE1F5KLafEW6V5U480q_NQ1YLphELoflVbNZtygtetHPUjRge-_VP81SKfl6sIKIawNmneZkGLqpOiEbNU4qVGpXk2TEqsCpgR4LOlsywYFXjYHutMTztalvSGzlXJk1v9icmZyvq6rvVM9V5sxvh1Mzm8kJmdKzhL_iAgX39GTjZ5_OHmwDgnLzV2q5PlxJl8d8Aj2pJtvlgJPgVee_ydSLUctTM7NafxxIRFmPTAlHrtF-jew_OzWp5F_AwAA___7NI-4) "one of our nation's largest untapped natural resources," according to Element3 founder and CEO Hood Whitson. The facility will initially produce 3,000 tons of lithium carbonate a year, but the company plans to increase output to 10,000 tons within the next two years. Currently, the U.S. produces nearly 6,500 tons of lithium carbonate a year. Maj. Gen. John Olson, the former chief technology officer for the U.S. Space Force, hailed the development for its economic and national security implications, calling it "a crowning example of the future." Abbott [praised the achievement](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkDGO2zAQRU9DdTQokpasgkUadZs2pTAkx-tBKFLgjHfl2wcOcoP0Hx_vvV8f2wdQofr5E3YMct7bVvGbC4pg3wrJg577UaBKO7Ayp2cEqrxZYydtrDbLloHKa_NDDtHkZRwwjPNsJnfzkx8e4RqNueZxHk2y83VyDqLPzqc5zfaO1g0U3mfGmmW0ZjT24m-Lv3nv_LJ4Ez0qbzCTtH6RBwqewPfyal_YL6ntQwkPkYOV-6HsquyaoRRgPI-OzO-Fsmt8MlVk1jv03yis7IoFd6zidEduz56Q9YF9J6g6AlPV_9w1ntIhCbWqoWadoMdWQVDfIVEheSm7Dj3k45tKIZ5m5c3nDlT-0sn_Nf0K9k8AAAD__zbmjwI) as "the epitome of quintessential Texas ingenuity."

He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw

Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw
Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

**Chapter 17 - The Wilderness**
When I told friends I was running for President, the most common response was something like, "Of what, your Co-op Board?" People were not encouraging. Maybe they had talked to my Mom.
Perhaps I wasn't as cool as I'd thought?
One friend said something I appreciated a great deal. "That seems crazy. But I said you were crazy before and you proved me wrong. So I said to myself after that, 'Okay, whatever Andrew tells you he's doing, just say yes.' So this time, I'm in."
I officially declared my presidential run in February 2018 with an article in the New York Times called, "His 2020 Campaign Message: The Robots are Coming."
It did not take the world by storm.
I make the same mistake over and over again: I think the next thing is going to be like the last thing.
I thought running for President was going to be something like starting a wholesome entrepreneurship non-profit; you talk to people, make your case, present a vision, and get people on board.
But running for President was much more about me and who I was. I initially wanted to call the campaign "UBI2020," for Universal Basic Income. But someone said, "That sounds like a urinary tract infection." "Yang2020" was much better, though that required me to be the frontman and own it.
Try something for me: find a roommate or friend or your spouse, take them by the shoulders and say to them, "I'm running for President of the United States of America."
It feels ridiculous, right? Like you immediately want to follow it up with, "I'm just kidding! This book asked me to say it to you, it's not real!"
It felt that way for me too for quite a while. And the reactions didn't help.
It took me about a year to be able to say it to a stranger with a straight face without any hint of irony or self-deprecation or doubt. For the most part it was incredibly awkward. I would go to my kids' school events and avoid questions about what I did for a living because saying, "I'm a presidential candidate" made me seem like an absolute lunatic. Imagine some Dad at the potluck telling you that? Plus, if you do decide to tell them, it takes 15 minutes to explain, and at the end they never say, "Let me help! Where do I donate or volunteer?"
Instead, I'd get a confused, "Interesting . . . good luck with that." Who wants to have that conversation over and over again?
Running for President without the virtues of fame, title, fortune, crowd support, social media following, etc. was a real education in humility. We had events where no one showed up. Who wants to hear from the random guy with delusions of grandeur?
Not many people it turns out.
So how did we get through those early days?
You take it day by day. But we had some things going for us. First, we had a fun, scrappy young team of true believers. Who would sign up for the Yang campaign as a wise career choice? Everyone on staff was driven by the truth of the message. Thanks to Zach in particular.
Second, we had a sense of humor about our situation. We didn't take ourselves that seriously.
Third, we seized on anything positive and made a big deal out of it. Anytime someone donated to our campaign, even if it was $5, we would ring a bell in our little office. I would then email or call that person to thank them. For a long time, I was thanking friends of mine, who totally deserved it! But sometimes I'd be thanking a stranger, and they seemed surprised and thrilled to hear from me. Pretty soon the newcomers outnumbered the people I knew.
Zach told me to get good at social media, because it was free. I put energy into that. That would eventually help us grow.
We said yes to any interview or event, no matter how small or niche-y. Ask me anything chat on Reddit? Sure! Interview with a tech website? Definitely. And then we thanked them and amplified it even if they were slightly snarky in the coverage.
One question I would get a lot in those early interviews:
"Are you serious? Do you think you can win?"
It's a bit of a trick question because if you say "Yes," you're crazy.
But if you say "No," you're a joke.
So you have to come up with a third answer, something like:
"This is a campaign of ideas." or
"There are multiple versions of victory."
If there were a few phrases I would use to sum up running for President in those early days, they were "camera angles," "rental cars,' and "rest stops."
Let's say we had a campaign event in South Carolina. 10 people showed up. If you pile those 10 people into the same picture plus yourself plus maybe a staffer or two, you could make it look like an okay event if . . . you get the right camera angle. With the wrong camera angle, it looks desolate and empty. So a lot of energy was spent arranging people and trying to get the right angle. A dud becomes a quality pic with the caption: "Talking to voters in Columbia, South Carolina - they're excited about the campaign!"
I spent a ton of time in rental cars. In Iowa and New Hampshire, they are the only ways to get around. At one point, my cameraperson was doubling as my driver. It was late at night in Iowa heading to our hotel, and he almost hit a divider. He was not inspiring confidence, despite being stone cold sober. Trying not to be obnoxious, I asked offhandedly, "Hey, out of curiosity, have you ever been in any car accidents?"
"Yeah, 4, but none of them were my fault."
I paused. "Great. Can you stop at this next gas station? I could use a bathroom break." Then, after I came out, I said, "Hey, I feel like driving. Just to relax. Can I take it from here?" There was no way I was going to wake up in a ditch because my cameraperson couldn't drive.
Because you're crisscrossing these states so much, the rest stops become havens. A lot of the time, because of your schedule, you're eating rest stop food as a meal, which isn't great. I got super excited to head into a rest stop to pick up a meal of mixed nuts, sunflower seeds, a KIND bar and popcorn with some iced tea. My favorite rest stop chain name in Iowa was Kum N Go, which had its name changed in 2023. I wonder why? It pains me that I will never go into a Kum N Go again.
People ask me how I had the perseverance to run. Sometimes I ask entrepreneurs, "If you were to decide to start a business, how much time have you just signed up for?"
They think for a minute. Then they typically answer,
"Five years."
"Eight years?"
"I don't know. Because you can't know."
"That's right! That means running for office is easier than starting a business." I respond. By deciding to run for President, I knew I was signing up for 3 years of campaigning. More likely it was going to be 2-and-a-half years since I probably wouldn't get past the primaries. "If I told you that you'd have to knock yourself out and do everything right for 2.5 years, could you do it?"
That made it seem more doable.
The moment I told my friends I was running and took a dollar from them, I signed up to do my utmost through the finish line. In the tough early days, I tried to make each day a little better than the one before. I believed in the case I was making because I knew it had the virtue of being true - AI was coming. I had to let people know. I was like Jon Snow except I knew who my parents were.
